question:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=F(x,y)$ will be a homogeneous differential equation for which of the following functions?
(i) $F(x,y)=3x+2y$
(ii) $F(x,y)=\sin\frac{y}{x}+\log~y-\log~x$
(iii) $F(x,y)=e^{y/x}+1$
(iv) $F(x,y)=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}-y$
explanation:
Step 1 Recall the definition of a homogeneous differential equation. An equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=F(x,y)$ is homogeneous if $F(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree 0. This is verified by checking whether $F(\lambda x,\lambda y)=F(x,y)$.

Step 2 For (i), $F(\lambda x,\lambda y)=3\lambda x+2\lambda y=\lambda(3x+2y)$, so it is homogeneous of degree 1, not degree 0.

Step 3 For (ii), $F(x,y)=\sin(y/x)+\log(y/x)$. Hence $F(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\sin(y/x)+\log(y/x)=F(x,y)$, so it is homogeneous of degree 0.

Step 4 For (iii), $F(\lambda x,\lambda y)=e^{(\lambda y)/(\lambda x)}+1=e^{y/x}+1=F(x,y)$, so it is homogeneous of degree 0.

Step 5 For (iv), $F(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-\lambda y=\lambda F(x,y)$, so it is homogeneous of degree 1. Therefore, only (ii) and (iii) satisfy the condition.
